images.caption:
Bound for Devil's Bridge. No. 8 sets off on the Vale of Rheidol Railway to Devil's Bridge with a special.  On the left are the former standard gauge engine sheds, now the main works and storage for the VoRR.
The Vale of Rheidol train is running along the alignment of the ex-Manchester and Milford Railway standard gauge line to Camarthen which closed in 1965.  At that time the Vale of Rheidol line followed a different route into Aberyswyth.  In the 1970's it was diverted on to the last mile or so of the Camarthen line trackbed and in to the former standard gauge platforms as seen today.

images.caption: Aberystwyth Harbour Quay The track of the Vale of Rheidol harbour branch ran along the quay here until it closed in the 1920's through lack of traffic. Timber and silver-lead ore were transshipped to quayside ships from the railway wagons. There has never been any indication of a run round loop anywhere on the branch so the wagons would need to have been propelled along the short line.

images.filename: 9¼ Milepost, Vale of Rheidol Railway - geograph.org.uk - 690104.jpg
images.caption: 9¼ Milepost, Vale of Rheidol Railway 9¼ miles from Aberystwyth. 'Original' artefacts are now few and far between on the Vale of Rheidol Railway. This milepost, a few yards north west of Rheidol Falls station, is probably of Great Western or British Railways origin. Interestingly, after the Aberystwyth terminus was relocated into the main line station in 1968, all of the mileposts were rendered inaccurate as the line became about 1000 feet shorter and they were never adjusted accordingly.
images.alt: 9¼ Milepost, Vale of Rheidol Railway 9¼ miles from Aberystwyth. 'Original' artefacts are now few and far between on the Vale of Rheidol Railway. images.caption: The half-timbered Old Market Hall stands at the crossroads of the four streets of the original medieval town. Built around 1600, it is the only surviving building of this type in Wales. Assize courts were held in the hall around 1605, and John Wesley preached from a pulpit stone on the open ground floor in 1748.
